content: The development of the World Health Organization (WHO) immunization policy and strategic guidance is a meticulous process that involves the application of evidence-based methodologies. These methods are implemented by the Strategic Advisory Group of Experts on Immunization (SAGE) to ensure that recommendations are grounded in the most reliable and up-to-date scientific evidence. The guidance is published under the copyright of the WHO, with specific terms allowing for non-commercial use, adaptation, and redistribution, provided proper citation is given. However, the use of the WHO logo is prohibited, and any adaptations must be licensed under equivalent Creative Commons terms. Translations of the work must include a disclaimer stating that the translation was not created by WHO and that the original English version remains the authoritative edition. The WHO emphasizes that its immunization policies and recommendations are not endorsements of specific organizations, products, or services. The organization also disclaims liability for any damages arising from the use of its published materials. The guidance document is intended to serve as a reference manual for those involved in the development of global and national immunization policies, including public health officials, immunization program managers, and members of technical advisory groups. It is also relevant to researchers and health professionals working in vaccine policy and strategy development. Vaccines are recognized as one of the most effective public health interventions, having saved millions of lives and prevented significant disability. Despite the availability of vaccines, their appropriate use requires guidance and leadership, which WHO provides through its evidence-based recommendations. These recommendations are informed by systematic reviews of contemporary research findings and are developed using internationally recognized methods and best practices. The WHO's commitment to evidence-based public health ensures that decisions are informed by the best available scientific evidence, while also considering factors such as equity, feasibility, affordability, sustainability, and stakeholder acceptability. The Immunization Agenda 2030 (IA2030), endorsed by all WHO Member States, outlines a global vision and strategy for vaccines and immunization for the decade 2021–2030. It positions immunization as a fundamental right and a critical investment in global health, aiming to create a healthier, safer, and more prosperous world. Strengthening evidence-based decision-making, with input from national immunization technical advisory groups (NITAGs), is a key focus area under IA2030. This includes ensuring that immunization policies and services are integrated throughout the life course, including catch-up vaccinations and booster doses. SAGE, as the principal advisory group to WHO on vaccines and immunization, provides guidance on global policies and strategies. It considers the entire spectrum of immunization activities, from research and development to implementation and delivery, and reports directly to the WHO Director-General. SAGE comprises at least 15 internationally recognized experts in immunization and related disciplines, selected through an open nomination process. Members serve in a personal, voluntary capacity and are not representatives of any government or organization. They adhere to WHO's rules on declarations of interest and receive no remuneration for their service. SAGE's recommendations are based on a comprehensive benefit-risk assessment and consider contextual factors such as feasibility, acceptability, epidemiological influences, equity, and cost-effectiveness. Recommendations typically apply to a class of vaccines with similar characteristics and performance profiles, although product-specific guidance may be issued in exceptional cases, such as during public health emergencies of international concern (PHEIC). SAGE's advice is presented to the WHO Director-General for approval before being published as global immunization guidance. SAGE working groups are time-limited advisory groups established to conduct in-depth reviews on specific topics. These groups consist of SAGE members and external subject-matter experts, selected to ensure a balance of technical expertise, geographical representation, and gender diversity. Working groups prepare independent evaluations of scientific and technical evidence and provide policy options for consideration by SAGE. They also identify knowledge gaps and research questions, including assessments of vaccine products under development. The SAGE secretariat, based at WHO headquarters in Geneva, supports SAGE and its working groups. It is led by the SAGE Executive Secretary and includes technical, administrative, and project management staff. The secretariat liaises with regional immunization technical advisory groups (RITAGs) and supports NITAGs. RITAGs operate in each of the six WHO regions, providing regional directors with technical advice on immunization-related matters.
